title: Swings and pendulums: what changes how fast they swing

summary.text: A swing, a hanging bunch of keys and the weight in an old wall clock all go back and forth in the same way. Each one is a pendulum: a weight hanging from a fixed point, free to swing. In this unit you build one from a thread and a bag of coins, and time 10 swings. You find that more coins or a wider start change the time very little, but a shorter thread makes the swings quicker. That steady beat is why pendulums were used to make the first accurate clocks.
summary.art: A child at a dining table timing a bag of coins swinging on a thread from a ruler, with a playground swing and an old pendulum wall clock drawn faintly behind.

intro.hook: Hold a bunch of keys by its ring and let the keys hang. Pull them a little to one side and let go. They swing back and forth by themselves. Now try a tiny push and then a big push. Does the big push make each swing quicker, or only wider?
intro.text: Anything that hangs from one point and swings back and forth is a pendulum. Swings, cradles, jhumkas and the keys in your hand are all pendulums. In this unit you find out what makes a pendulum swing quickly or slowly. Make a guess now, and keep it. You will test it soon.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a ring of keys that swing back and forth, with a faint curved arrow showing the swing.

outcomes: I can name the parts of a pendulum, the pivot, the string and the bob, and say what one full swing is.
I can explain why a pendulum swings back after I let it go, and say where it moves fastest.
I can plan a fair test that changes one thing at a time, and time 10 full swings.
I can say that a shorter string makes a pendulum swing quicker, and that more weight or a wider start change the time very little.
I can explain why a swing slows down and stops, and why pushing at the right moment makes it go higher.
I can say how pendulums are used in clocks and metronomes, and how gibbons and our own legs swing like pendulums.

terms.meaning: A weight that hangs from a fixed point and can swing freely back and forth.
terms.example: A playground swing is a pendulum. So is a bag of coins hanging on a thread.
terms.art: A bag of coins hanging on a thread from a ruler, with a curved arrow showing the swing.

terms.meaning: The fixed point a pendulum hangs from. The pendulum swings around it.
terms.example: On a swing, the pivot is the hook or bar at the top of the chains.
terms.art: The top bar of a playground swing, with a circle around the hooks the chains hang from.

terms.meaning: The weight at the bottom of a pendulum.
terms.example: In this unit the bob is a small bag of coins. On a swing, the bob is you.
terms.art: A small plastic bag twisted tight around five coins, tied to a thread.

terms.meaning: The pendulum goes from where you let it go, over to the far side, and back again. Scientists call the time this takes the period.
terms.example: A 50 cm pendulum takes about one and a half seconds for one full swing.
terms.art: A pendulum drawn three times: at the start on the left, at the far right, and back at the left, with arrows showing there and back.

terms.meaning: To move back and forth again and again, over the same path.
terms.example: A swing oscillates. So does a guitar string, much faster.
terms.art: A swing shown at both ends of its path, with a double-headed arrow between them.

terms.meaning: The force that pulls everything towards the Earth.
terms.example: Gravity pulls the bob down, so it always swings back towards the middle.
terms.art: A pendulum pulled to one side, with a small arrow pointing straight down from the bob.

terms.meaning: The push of the air against anything that moves through it. It slows moving things down.
terms.example: A pendulum with a big card taped to it stops swinging much sooner, because the card pushes against more air.
terms.art: Two pendulums side by side, one with a flat card taped on it and tiny lines of air bending around the card.

terms.meaning: The grip between two things that rub together. It slows movement down.
terms.example: A squeaky swing loses its swing faster, because its hooks rub on the bar.
terms.art: The hook of a swing rubbing on a metal bar, with small heat lines.

terms.meaning: When small pushes come at the same beat as a thing's own swing, each push adds to the last, and the swing grows big.
terms.example: Pushing a friend on a swing each time they come back to you makes them go higher and higher.
terms.art: A parent pushing a child on a swing at the moment the swing comes back towards them.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same, so you know what made the difference.
terms.example: To test the weight, change only the number of coins. Keep the same thread length and the same start.
terms.art: Two pendulums of the same length side by side, one with one coin and one with five coins.

terms.meaning: A tool that ticks at a steady beat, to help musicians keep time. Many have a swinging arm that works like an upside-down pendulum.
terms.example: A veena student practises with a metronome so that each note comes exactly on the beat.
terms.art: A wooden metronome with a swinging arm and a small sliding weight on it.

explanations.context: This card says what a pendulum is and names its parts.
explanations.definition: A pendulum is a weight, called the bob, that hangs from a fixed point, called the pivot, and is free to swing back and forth.
explanations.description: A pendulum has three parts. The pivot is the fixed point at the top. The string, chain or rod hangs from the pivot. The bob is the weight at the bottom. When the bob is still, it hangs straight down. Pull it to one side and let go, and it swings back and forth over the same path. One full swing is there and back, from where you let go to the far side and back again.
examples: A playground swing: the bar is the pivot, the chains are the string and the child is the bob.
A thottil, the cloth cradle that families in Kerala and Tamil Nadu hang from the ceiling.
A jhumka earring swinging as you turn your head.
The long swinging rod with a brass disc in an old wall clock.
explanations.art: A pendulum with three labels: pivot at the top, string, and bob at the bottom, next to a swing labelled the same way.

explanations.concept: Why a pendulum swings back and forth
explanations.context: When you let go of a pendulum, why does it not just stop at the bottom? This card explains.
explanations.definition: Gravity pulls the bob down towards the middle. When it reaches the middle it is moving fast, so it carries on up the other side until gravity slows it to a stop. Then it falls back, and the swing repeats.
explanations.description: When you pull the bob to one side, you lift it a little. Let go, and gravity pulls it down and back towards the middle. It goes faster and faster on the way down. At the very bottom it is moving fastest. A moving thing keeps moving unless something slows it, so the bob does not stop in the middle. It swings up the other side. Now gravity slows it down, until it stops for a moment at the far end. Then it falls back the other way. Each swing, its speed turns into height, and its height turns back into speed.
examples: On a swing, you feel your tummy flip at the bottom, where you move fastest.
At the very top of each swing, a swing stops for a moment before it comes back.
A bag of coins on a thread comes back almost to the same height it started from.
explanations.art: A pendulum drawn at five points of a swing, with long speed arrows at the bottom and no arrow at the two ends.

explanations.concept: What changes the swing time: the length
explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the swing test: which change made the swings quicker or slower.
explanations.definition: The time for one full swing depends on the length of the pendulum. A shorter pendulum swings quicker. A longer one swings slower. For small swings, the weight of the bob and how wide it starts change the time very little.
explanations.description: In the swing test, 5 coins and 1 coin both took about 14 seconds for 10 swings. A small start and a wide start took about 14 seconds too. But a thread one quarter as long took only about 7 seconds. Make a pendulum 4 times shorter, and it swings twice as fast. Weight does not matter for the same reason that a heavy and a light ball fall together. Gravity pulls a heavier bob harder, but a heavier bob also needs more force to get moving. The two cancel out. A wider start also takes nearly the same time, because the bob falls from higher and so moves faster over its longer path. Length is measured from the pivot to the middle of the bob, because that is where the weight is.
examples: A pendulum 25 cm long takes about 1 second for one full swing. One 1 metre long takes about 2 seconds.
A small child and a grown-up on the same swing take about the same time for each swing.
The swing for little children, with short ropes, swings back and forth quicker than a tall swing.
explanations.art: Three pendulums side by side: a long one swinging slowly, a short one swinging quickly, and a long one with a heavier bob swinging at the same pace as the first.

explanations.concept: Very wide swings take a little longer
explanations.context: Is a small swing and a wide swing really the same? This card tells the small exception.
explanations.definition: For swings up to about a hand-width or two, the time hardly changes. A very wide swing, high up to the side, takes a little longer than a small one.
explanations.description: Galileo thought every swing takes exactly the same time, however wide. Later, Christiaan Huygens worked out that this is only nearly true. A pendulum let go from far out to the side, almost level with the pivot, takes about one sixth longer for each swing than a small one. For the swings in your test, the difference is only a few tenths of a second in 10 swings. That is about as much as a stopwatch press can be off by. This is why clock pendulums swing only a little way each side.
examples: In the swing test, the wide start may take 14.4 seconds and the small start 14.2 seconds.
A wall clock's pendulum swings only a few centimetres each way.
explanations.art: Two pendulums of the same length, one with a tiny swing and one swinging up almost level with the pivot, with a clock face next to each.

explanations.concept: Why a swing slows down and stops
explanations.context: A pendulum does not swing for ever. This card explains what stops it.
explanations.definition: A pendulum slows down because air resistance pushes against the bob and string, and friction acts at the pivot. Each swing loses a little movement, which ends up as a tiny bit of warmth in the air and the pivot.
explanations.description: If nothing slowed it, a pendulum would swing for ever. But it moves through air, and the air pushes back. A bob with a big flat card on it pushes more air out of the way, so it slows down much sooner. At the top, the string or the swing's hooks rub on the pivot, and that friction slows it too. A heavy, small bob on a thin thread keeps swinging longest. The swing gets narrower and narrower, but each swing still takes about the same time.
examples: A swing in a park stops on its own after a minute or two if nobody pushes it.
A bag of coins on a thread swings for minutes. The same bag with a postcard taped on it stops in under a minute.
explanations.art: A pendulum with a flat card swinging, with tiny air lines pushing against the card, and a smaller and smaller arc drawn behind it.

explanations.concept: Pushing at the right moment: resonance
explanations.context: How do you make a swing go higher with only small pushes? This card explains.
explanations.definition: Every pendulum has its own beat, set by its length. Small pushes that come at that same beat add up, and the swing grows big. This is called resonance.
explanations.description: When you push a friend on a swing, you push each time they come back to you. Each push adds a little to the swing. Because the pushes come at the swing's own beat, they add up, and your friend goes higher and higher. If you push at the wrong moment, while the swing is still coming towards you, you slow it down instead. You can try this with your coin pendulum. Hold the top of the thread and move your hand a tiny bit side to side, in time with the swing. The swing grows. Move your hand too fast or too slow, and it stays small.
examples: Pushing a swing each time it comes back to you.
Children on an Onam oonjal swing higher by leaning and pulling in time with each swing.
Soldiers break step when they march across a bridge, so their steps don't add up to shake it.
explanations.art: A child pushing a swing just as it reaches the back of its path, with a small push arrow and a growing curved path drawn above.

explanations.concept: How pendulums keep time in clocks
explanations.context: Why were pendulums used in clocks? This card explains.
explanations.definition: A pendulum of a fixed length always takes the same time for each swing, so a clock can count its swings to measure time. A small part of the clock gives the pendulum a tiny push on each swing, so it never dies down.
explanations.description: In 1656, Christiaan Huygens made the first pendulum clock. Each swing of the pendulum lets a toothed wheel turn on by one tooth, and that is the tick. The wheel, in turn, gives the pendulum a tiny push each time, so it keeps swinging. The wheels count the ticks and turn the hands. If a pendulum clock runs slow, you shorten the pendulum a little. Most have a small nut under the bob. Turn it to move the bob up, and the clock goes faster. A pendulum about 1 metre long takes one second to swing one way. Tall floor clocks use pendulums this long.
examples: Old wall clocks in many Indian homes have a long pendulum behind a glass door.
A metronome is a pendulum turned upside down. Sliding its weight up makes it tick more slowly.
The pendulum in a tall floor clock is about 1 metre long, so each tick is one second.
explanations.art: The inside of a wall clock: a long pendulum with a brass disc and a nut underneath, and a toothed wheel at the top that moves one tooth with each swing.

explanations.concept: Living things that swing like pendulums
explanations.context: Living things use pendulum swings too. This card tells how gibbons and people do it.
explanations.definition: Some animals move by letting parts of their body swing like a pendulum, because a swing moves them forward without much effort.
explanations.description: Hoolock gibbons are India's only apes. They live high in the forests of Assam and the north-east. They need to travel far through the treetops to find ripe fruit, without coming down to the ground, where it is less safe. Their arms are very long and strong. A gibbon hangs from one arm and swings forward like a pendulum, then grabs the next branch with the other hand. Gravity does much of the work, so this way of travelling saves energy. Your own legs swing like pendulums when you walk. A short leg swings forward quicker than a long one, so small children take quicker steps than grown-ups.
examples: A gibbon swinging from branch to branch, one arm at a time.
A child walking next to a grown-up takes more steps to cover the same path.
explanations.art: A hoolock gibbon hanging from a branch by one long arm, swinging forward towards the next branch, with a curved arrow showing the swing.

agreed.text: A pendulum's time for one swing depends on its length. A shorter pendulum swings quicker.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can time a short and a long pendulum at home. Scientists have measured it very exactly since the 1600s.

agreed.text: For small swings, the weight of the bob does not change the time of a swing.
agreed.evidence: Galileo swung lead and cork balls side by side. Isaac Newton tested pendulum bobs filled with gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, salt, wood, water and wheat, and found the same time for all.

agreed.text: Small swings and slightly wider swings take nearly the same time. Very wide swings take a little longer.
agreed.evidence: Christiaan Huygens worked this out in 1673, and careful timing shows it.

agreed.text: A pendulum slows down because of air resistance and friction at the pivot.
agreed.evidence: A pendulum swinging in a box with the air pumped out keeps swinging far longer than one in air.

agreed.text: The same pendulum swings more slowly where gravity is weaker.
agreed.evidence: Pendulum clocks run slightly slow near the equator and on high mountains, where gravity is a little weaker. On the Moon, a pendulum would swing about two and a half times more slowly.

challenging.who: A very common first guess, from children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Heavy things feel more powerful. A heavier swing is also harder to stop.
challenging.against: In the swing test, 1 coin and 5 coins took about the same time for 10 swings. Gravity pulls a heavy bob harder, but it also needs more force to move, and the two cancel.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that weight changes how fast a pendulum swings.

challenging.claim: A bigger push makes each swing quicker.
challenging.who: Many children, when they first push a swing
challenging.for: A big push makes the swing move faster at the bottom, so it seems each swing should take less time.
challenging.against: The swing moves faster, but it also travels further. The two balance out, so each swing takes nearly the same time. Only very wide swings take a little longer.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that pushing harder makes a swing go back and forth quicker.

challenging.claim: Every swing, however wide, takes exactly the same time.
challenging.for: For small swings, timing by hand shows no difference at all.
challenging.against: Christiaan Huygens showed in 1673 that very wide swings take a little longer. Clockmakers keep swings small for this reason.
challenging.context: This card is about a great scientist's idea that turned out to be nearly true, but not exactly.

challenging.claim: Once a pendulum starts, it should keep swinging for ever.
challenging.who: Some people who see a clock pendulum that never seems to stop
challenging.for: A clock's pendulum keeps swinging day after day.
challenging.against: A clock gives its pendulum a tiny push every swing. Without it, air resistance and friction at the pivot slow any pendulum down until it stops.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a pendulum on its own could swing for ever.

big_questions.q: A heavy bob is pulled harder by gravity, yet it swings in the same time as a light one. What else about the heavy bob balances the stronger pull?
big_questions.hint: Think about which is harder to get moving: a full trolley or an empty one.

big_questions.q: A wide swing travels much further than a small one. How can it take almost the same time?
big_questions.hint: Watch where the bob moves fastest in a wide swing and in a small one.

big_questions.q: Why does a shorter pendulum swing quicker?
big_questions.hint: Think about how far the bob has to travel, and how steep its path is near the ends.

big_questions.q: Your heart, your breathing and your steps all have their own beat. Is a heartbeat a kind of pendulum?
big_questions.hint: A pendulum swings back to the middle again and again. What brings a heartbeat back each time?

big_questions.q: On the Moon, the same pendulum swings more slowly. Would a pendulum clock on the Moon still tell the right time?
big_questions.hint: A clock only counts swings. What would happen if each swing took longer?

big_questions.q: Before clocks, people told the time by the Sun, the stars and their own rhythms. What changed when everyone could count the same seconds?
big_questions.hint: Think about trains, school bells and phone calls.

story.title: The Onam Swing
story.note: The story is made up. The swing science in it is true: a heavy and a light rider take about the same time for each swing, a shorter rope swings quicker, and a pendulum clock is put right by moving its bob up or down with the nut beneath it. Families in Kerala really do hang an oonjal, a swing, for Onam.
text: Every Onam, Ammamma's house in Thrissur fills up with cousins. This year Meenu was nine, and her cousin Arjun was seven.

On the first morning, Valyachan, their uncle, climbed a ladder into the old mango tree. He tied two thick ropes to a high branch and fixed a flat wooden plank between them. It was the Onam oonjal, the swing that families in Kerala hang up for the festival.
Arjun jumped on first. Meenu pushed him, and back and forth he went, while the mango leaves shook above him. "Higher!" he shouted.
"My turn next," said Valyachan. "I'm the heaviest, so I'll swing the fastest."
Arjun shook his head. "No, you'll be the slowest. Heavy things are slow, like a loaded lorry."

Meenu had an idea. "Let's find out," she said. "Ammamma's clock in the hall ticks once every second. I'll count the ticks while the rider counts swings." She stood by the open window, where she could hear the clock.
Arjun went first. Meenu let him go from her hands and said, "Zero!" Each time the swing came back to her, Arjun counted one more. When he shouted "Ten!", Meenu had counted 30 ticks.
Then Valyachan sat on the plank. The ropes creaked. Meenu pulled him back to the same place and let go. When he reached ten swings, she had counted 29 ticks.
"One less! So I am faster," said Valyachan.
"One tick is only me counting a bit late," said Meenu. "Twenty-nine and thirty are almost the same. Let's try Ammamma."
Ammamma laughed, but she sat down carefully on the plank, holding the ropes. Ten swings took 30 ticks.

Arjun frowned. "Then it must be the push. Push me really hard this time, Meenu." Meenu pulled the swing back as far as she could reach and let go. Arjun flew high, squealing. Ten swings took 31 ticks.
"A tiny bit slower," said Meenu, "even though you went much higher. The big push made you go further and faster. But each swing still took about the same time."

The next day, the little cousins wanted a swing of their own. Valyachan tied a second swing to a low branch, with ropes only as long as Meenu was tall. Arjun sat on it, and Meenu counted again. Ten swings took only 20 ticks.
"It's the rope!" said Meenu. "A short rope makes a quick swing. A long rope makes a slow swing. Heavy or light, big push or small push, the beat hardly changes. Only the length changes it."

That evening, Ammamma looked up at the clock in the hall and sighed. "This clock has been losing time," she said. "By Sunday it is five minutes behind. Your Appooppan, your grandfather, used to fix it. I never learned how."
Meenu opened the clock's glass door. Inside, a long rod swung slowly back and forth, with a round brass disc at the bottom. Under the disc was a small nut on a screw.
"The clock counts the swings of this pendulum," said Meenu. "Each swing makes one tick. If the clock is slow, the pendulum must be swinging too slowly. So we need it a little shorter."
Ammamma held the rod still while Meenu turned the nut. The brass disc moved up, just a few millimetres.
"Such a tiny change?" asked Arjun.
"The swing ropes changed a lot, so the beat changed a lot," said Meenu. "The clock is only a little slow, so it needs only a little change."

Ammamma set the hands to match her phone, and Meenu gave the pendulum a small push to start it again. Over the next two days, they checked the clock against the phone every morning and every night. The first day it was still a minute slow, so Meenu turned the nut once more. After that, it kept time with the phone.
On the last night of Onam, Arjun lay on his mat in the hall and listened to the clock. Tick, tock. Tick, tock.
"Meenu," he whispered. "The clock is a swing too. It's just a very small one, swinging all night."
"And it keeps the same beat, whoever is listening," said Meenu, half asleep.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a pendulum's time for each swing is set by its length. A heavier rider or a bigger push changes it very little, and a very wide swing takes only slightly longer. A pendulum clock is put right by making the pendulum a tiny bit shorter, to speed it up, or longer, to slow it down.
ask: Valyachan was heavier than Arjun. Did he swing faster? How did Meenu find out?
Why did Meenu say that 29 ticks and 30 ticks were almost the same?
Why did the little cousins' swing go back and forth so much quicker?
The clock was slow. Why did Meenu move the brass disc up and not down?
Arjun said the clock is a swing too. Is he right? What is the same, and what is different?

games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows a pendulum. Players guess which pendulum swings quickest, using what they found in the swing test.

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and deal 4 to each player. With one player, deal 4 to yourself and 4 to an empty chair, and play both hands.
Each round, every player puts one card face up.
The pendulum with the shortest string or chain swings quickest and wins the round.
Weight and start do not count. If two cards have the same length, they tie and share the point.
A trick card has the same length as the last card played, so it ties with it.
Before the cards are judged, each player says which card they think wins, and why. A right guess with a reason scores 1 extra point.
Play until the cards run out. Most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Deal 4 to each player. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card shows a pendulum. The quickest swing wins the round. Think about what you found in the swing test.
flow.kid: Take 4 cards. Each one is a pendulum. The quickest swing wins.
flow.context: This is the start of Quick or Slow, a card game about which pendulums swing quickest.

flow.do: Play a practice round with two cards: 'String 50 cm, bob 1 coin' and 'String 50 cm, bob 5 coins, wide start'.

check.q: Two pendulums are both 50 cm long. One has 1 coin. The other has 5 coins and a wide start. Which swings quicker?
options: They take about the same time
check.why: Both strings are 50 cm, so both swing at about the same beat. The extra coins and the wider start change the time very little. If you picked one, think back to the swing test, where 1 coin and 5 coins both took about 14 seconds.

flow.do: Play the rounds. Before judging each round, ask each player to say which card wins and why.
flow.say: Before we judge, tell me which card wins. Give your reason.
flow.kid: Put down a card. Say which one wins, and why.

ask.q: Why does the jhumka card beat the temple bell card?
good: The jhumka hangs on a shorter hook, so it swings quicker.
3 cm is shorter than 20 cm.

flow.parent: Listen for the reason. 'It is lighter' is the idea the game is testing. Ask: what did the coins do in the swing test?

flow.do: Add up the points. Then pick the slowest card in the whole pack together.
flow.say: Which card in the whole pack is the slowest swinger? Why?
flow.kid: Find the slowest card in the pack. Why is it the slowest?

ask.q: Which is the slowest card, and why?

games.title: Pendulum Says: an acting game
games.context: This is an acting game. The caller reads a card, and everyone swings their arm like a pendulum of that kind, as quickly or slowly as it would really swing.

flow.kid: Listen to each card. Swing quicker, slower or the same.

check.q: The card says HEAVIER BOB! What should your swing do?
check.why: A heavier bob on the same string swings at the same beat. In the swing test, 1 coin and 5 coins took about the same time. If you changed your beat, remember that test.

flow.do: Try the real thing. Hold your arm straight and let it swing, then bend it at the elbow and let it swing.
flow.say: Now swing your straight arm, then your bent arm. Which one swings quicker by itself?
flow.kid: Swing your arm straight. Then bent. Which is quicker?

ask.q: Why does a bent arm swing quicker?
good: Bending makes it shorter.
A shorter pendulum swings quicker.

flow.parent: A bent arm is a shorter pendulum, so it swings quicker on its own. This is why runners bend their arms.

setup.art: A parent and a child standing in a living room, each letting one arm swing like a pendulum.
setup.caption: 1. Let one arm swing. Your shoulder is the pivot.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that says SHORT STRING while the others swing their arms quickly.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads a card, and everyone changes their swing.

experiments.title: The Swing Test: what changes how long a swing takes?
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a pendulum from a thread and a bag of coins. Then you change one thing at a time, and time 10 swings each time.
experiments.question: Does the weight of the bob, how wide it starts, or the length of the string change how long a pendulum takes to swing?
experiments.predict: We will change three things, one at a time: the number of coins, how wide the swing starts, and the length of the thread. Which ones will change the time for 10 swings? Will it get quicker or slower? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing in each test. Keep the same thread, the same kind of coins and the same pivot. Always count 10 full swings, and do each test twice, because one try can be off.
results_table: A big change, or about the same?

materials.item: strong sewing thread or thin string, about 1 metre
a 30 cm ruler, wooden, plastic or steel
3 heavy books, to hold the ruler down on the table
a small plastic bag, or a cut-off corner of a polythene bag
coins of one kind, such as 5 rupee coins
sticky tape
a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a measuring tape or a second ruler
a pencil and the results table on paper

experiments.safety: Keep faces away from the swinging bag. Put the books on firmly so the ruler cannot tip off the table.

schedule.what: Build a coin pendulum. Guess, then time 10 swings with 5 coins and 1 coin, a small and a wide start, and a long and a short thread.

experiments.record: Fill in the table as you go. At the end, circle the one change that made a big difference. Then write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the table with 10 cm sticking out over the edge. 2. Put the three books on the rest of it. 3. Put 5 coins in the bag, twist it tight and tie the thread round the twist. 4. Tie the other end to the tip of the ruler and tape it so it cannot slide. 5. Make the thread 50 cm long, from the ruler to the middle of the coins.
flow.say: We are building a pendulum. The ruler's tip is the pivot. The bag of coins is the bob. We measure the length to the middle of the coins, because that is where the weight is.
flow.kid: Hang the coin bag from the ruler. Make it 50 cm long. Measure to the middle of the coins.
flow.parent: Any coins work, but use one kind all through. The bag should hang about 20 cm above the floor. If the ruler bends or wobbles, add another book.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Swing Test. You build a pendulum from a ruler, a thread and a bag of coins.

flow.do: Show how to count. Pull the bag one hand-width to the side and let go. Say 'zero' as you let go. Say 'one' when it comes back to your hand, 'two' the next time, and so on up to 10.
flow.say: One full swing is there and back. We say zero as we let go. Then we count one each time it comes back to where it started.
flow.kid: Let go and say zero. Count one when it comes back. Count up to ten.

check.q: You let go of the bag. It swings to the far side and back to your hand. How many full swings is that?
check.why: One full swing is there and back. Many children count each side as one swing. That counts twice as many, so the times would not match anyone else's.

flow.do: Ask for guesses and reasons for each of the three tests, and write them in the table.
flow.say: First we will change the coins, then the start, then the length. Which will change the time for 10 swings? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will more coins change the time? A wider start? A shorter thread? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen with 1 coin instead of 5? Why?
good: Any guess with a reason, such as: it will swing quicker because it is lighter.

flow.parent: Don't say what will happen. Most children guess that weight or a bigger push changes the time. That is a good guess to test.

flow.do: 1. With 5 coins, pull the bag one hand-width out. 2. Start the stopwatch as you let go, and stop it at 'ten'. 3. Do it twice and write both times. 4. Take out 4 coins, leaving 1. Check the length is still 50 cm to the middle of the coin. 5. Time 10 swings twice again.
flow.say: Test one changes only the weight. Same length, same start. That makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Time 10 swings with 5 coins. Then with 1 coin. Do each one twice.
flow.parent: Each should take about 14 seconds. If two tries differ by more than 1 second, do a third. One person lets go and counts, the other works the stopwatch.

flow.do: 1. Put the 5 coins back. 2. Time 10 swings from one hand-width out, twice. 3. Time 10 swings from two big hand-widths out, about 25 cm, twice.
flow.say: Test two changes only how wide it starts. The wide swing goes much further. Will it take longer?
flow.kid: Time a small start. Then a wide start. Write both times.
flow.parent: Both should take about 14 seconds. The wide start may be a few tenths of a second longer. That small difference is real, and the explanation cards come back to it.

flow.do: 1. Wind the thread round the ruler's tip and tape it. 2. Stop when it is 12 and a half cm to the middle of the coins, a quarter of 50 cm. 3. Time 10 swings twice.
flow.say: Test three changes only the length. The thread is now a quarter as long. Count quickly, because it will be fast.
flow.kid: Make the thread short. Time 10 swings again. Count fast!
flow.parent: This should take about 7 seconds, half the time. Count out loud with your child, because the swings come quickly.

flow.do: Look at the whole table together. Circle the change that made a big difference.
flow.say: Which change made a big difference? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Which change made a big difference? Say what you think, what you saw and why.

good: What I think: only the length changes the swing time. What I saw: 1 coin and 5 coins both took about 14 seconds, but the short thread took 7. Why: the length sets the beat.

check.q: In your test, which change made the swings much quicker?
check.why: A shorter thread made 10 swings take about half the time. The coins and the wide start changed the time very little. If you picked another answer, look again at the numbers in your table.

experiments.title: The One-Second Pendulum
experiments.context: In this experiment you change the length of your coin pendulum until each full swing takes exactly one second.
experiments.question: How long must the thread be so that one full swing takes exactly 1 second?
experiments.predict: 50 cm took about 14 seconds for 10 swings. 12 and a half cm took about 7 seconds. What length will take exactly 10 seconds? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same 5 coins and the same small start every time. Change only the length. Always count 10 swings, so that small timing mistakes matter less.
results_table: Length (cm, to the middle of the coins)
Too slow, too quick or just right?

materials.item: strong sewing thread or thin string, about 1 metre
a 30 cm ruler, wooden, plastic or steel
3 heavy books, to hold the ruler down on the table
a small plastic bag, or a cut-off corner of a polythene bag
coins of one kind, such as 5 rupee coins
sticky tape
a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a measuring tape or a second ruler
a pencil and the results table on paper

experiments.safety: Keep faces away from the swinging bag.

schedule.what: Try lengths between 12 and 50 cm until 10 swings take 10 seconds.

experiments.record: Write every length you tried and its time. Draw a star by the length that took 10 seconds.

flow.do: Set up the coin pendulum as in the Swing Test. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: We want 10 swings to take exactly 10 seconds. What length do you think we need? Why?
flow.kid: Guess the length for 10 swings in 10 seconds. Why that length?

ask.q: What length do you guess, and why?
good: Between 12 and 50 cm, because 10 seconds is between 7 and 14.
About 30 cm, because it is in the middle.

flow.context: This is the first step of the One-Second Pendulum. You change the thread length until each swing takes one second.

flow.do: 1. Set the guessed length. 2. Time 10 swings. 3. If it took more than 10 seconds, make the thread shorter. If less, make it longer. 4. Repeat until it takes 10 seconds.
flow.say: Too slow? Make it shorter. Too quick? Make it longer. Change it a little at a time.
flow.kid: Time 10 swings. Too slow? Shorter. Too quick? Longer. Try again.
flow.parent: The answer is about 25 cm. Many children guess about 30 cm, halfway between. The length is not halfway, because halving the time needs a quarter of the length.

flow.do: Use your one-second pendulum to time something. Count swings while your child hops on one foot, or while they say a times table.
flow.say: Now our pendulum is a clock. Each full swing is one second. How long can you hop on one foot?
flow.kid: Your pendulum is a clock now. Count swings while you hop!

check.q: You made a pendulum that takes 1 second for each full swing. Your friend wants one that takes 2 seconds. What should she do?
check.why: A longer pendulum swings slower. In fact it must be 4 times as long, about 1 metre, to take twice the time. Adding coins changes the time very little.

setup.caption: 1. Hang a bag of coins from a ruler held down by books.

setup.caption: 2. Change the length until 10 swings take 10 seconds.

experiments.title: What Makes a Swing Die Down?
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out why a pendulum slows down and stops, by giving it a card that catches the air.
experiments.question: Does a pendulum that pushes more air stop swinging sooner?
experiments.predict: We will tape a postcard to the thread just above the coins. Will the pendulum with the card stop swinging sooner, later or at the same time? Will each swing take longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same length, the same coins and the same start for both. Change only the card. Stop the stopwatch at the same mark both times.
results_table: Seconds until it no longer reaches the 10 cm mark
Seconds for 10 swings at the start

materials.item: strong sewing thread or thin string, about 1 metre
a 30 cm ruler, wooden, plastic or steel
3 heavy books, to hold the ruler down on the table
a small plastic bag, or a cut-off corner of a polythene bag
coins of one kind, such as 5 rupee coins
sticky tape
a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a measuring tape or a second ruler
a pencil and the results table on paper
a postcard or a piece of thin card about the size of your hand
a shoebox or a stack of books to stand under the pendulum
a strip of paper about 50 cm long, such as two sheets taped end to end

experiments.safety: Keep faces away from the swinging bag.

schedule.what: Time how long the coin pendulum takes to die down, with and without a card.

experiments.record: Write both times. Draw the two pendulums and show with arrows where the air pushes.

flow.do: 1. Set up the 50 cm coin pendulum. 2. Put a shoebox under it, with a paper strip about 50 cm long on top. 3. Move the box until the strip's middle is right under the resting bag. 4. Mark 10 cm and 20 cm each side of the middle with a pencil.
flow.say: We let go from the 20 cm mark. We stop the clock when the bag no longer swings out as far as the 10 cm mark.
flow.kid: Let go from 20 cm. Watch it swing. When does it stop reaching 10 cm?
flow.context: This is the first step of the test on what makes a swing die down.

flow.do: Ask for guesses and reasons.
flow.say: Next we will tape a card on. Will the card make it die down sooner? Will each swing take longer? Why?
flow.kid: With a card, will it stop sooner? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What will the card do? Why?
good: Any guess with a reason, such as: it will stop sooner because the card pushes the air.

flow.do: 1. Let go from 20 cm and start the stopwatch. 2. Stop it when the bag no longer reaches 10 cm. 3. Write the time.
flow.say: This one may take a few minutes. Keep watching the 10 cm mark.
flow.kid: Let go. Watch the 10 cm mark. Stop the clock when it falls short.
flow.parent: Without a card it may take a minute or more. If your child gets bored, count swings out loud together.

flow.do: 1. Tape the card flat to the thread just above the coins, facing the way it swings. 2. Time 10 swings at the start. 3. Then time how long until it no longer reaches 10 cm.
flow.say: Now the card has to push the air out of the way on every swing.
flow.kid: Tape on the card. Time it again. What changed?
flow.parent: With the card it should die down in well under a minute. Each swing still takes about the same time, about 14 seconds for 10.

flow.do: Compare the times.
flow.say: What did the card change, and what did it not change? Why?
flow.kid: What did the card change? What stayed the same?

check.q: Why did the pendulum with the card die down sooner?
options: The air pushed against the big flat card
The card made the thread longer
check.why: The card pushes a lot of air out of the way, and the air pushes back. That is air resistance. A card weighs very little, so weight is not the reason.

setup.caption: 1. Hang a bag of coins from a ruler held down by books.

activities.title: Swinging Keys
activities.context: This is a quick start to the unit. You swing a bunch of keys and notice what they do.

materials.item: a bunch of keys on a ring, or any small heavy thing on a string

activities.safety: Swing gently, away from faces and glass.

schedule.what: Swing a bunch of keys. Notice and wonder. Make a guess to test later.

activities.record: Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.

flow.do: 1. Hold the key ring between finger and thumb so the keys hang down. 2. Pull them a little to one side and let go. 3. Watch together.
flow.say: Watch the keys. What do you notice? Where do they go fastest? Where do they stop?
flow.kid: Let the keys swing. What do you notice? Where are they fastest?

good: They swing back and forth.
They are fastest at the bottom.
They stop for a moment at each end.

flow.context: This is the first activity of the swings unit. You let a bunch of keys swing and watch closely.

flow.do: Give a tiny push, then a big push. Then hang the keys from a shoelace. Try the lace long, then short.
flow.say: Now a tiny push, then a big one. Does the big push make each swing quicker, or only wider?
flow.kid: Try a tiny push. Then a big push. Is the big one quicker?
flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Your child will test this properly in the Swing Test.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and write it down.
flow.say: What do you think changes how fast a swing goes back and forth? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What makes a swing quick or slow? Make a guess. Say why.

good: Any guess with a reason. Keep it for the Swing Test.

setup.art: A child's fingers holding a key ring with the keys hanging still.
setup.caption: 1. Let the keys hang.

setup.art: The keys swinging, with a curved arrow and a speed mark at the bottom of the swing.
setup.caption: 2. Pull them aside and let go. Watch.

activities.title: Push at the Right Time
activities.context: In this activity you make a pendulum swing high using tiny hand movements, if they come at the right beat. This is called resonance.

materials.item: the coin pendulum from the Swing Test, 50 cm long, held in your hand instead of tied to the ruler

schedule.what: Make a still pendulum swing high with tiny hand movements in time with its beat.

activities.record: Write what happened when you moved your hand in time, too fast and too slow.

flow.do: 1. Hold the top of the thread between finger and thumb, with the coin bag hanging still. 2. Move your hand very slightly side to side, no more than 1 cm, in time with the bag's own swing.
flow.say: Move your hand just a tiny bit, in time with the swing. Watch the bag.
flow.kid: Move your hand a tiny bit. Keep in time with the swing. Watch!
flow.parent: The bag should swing wider and wider within about 10 swings. If it doesn't, the hand movement is too big or too fast. Wait for the bag to come back before each movement.
flow.context: This is the first step of Push at the Right Time. You make a pendulum swing high with tiny hand movements.

flow.do: Stop the bag. Now move your hand quickly side to side, much faster than the swing.
flow.say: Now shake it fast. Does it swing high this time?
flow.kid: Now shake your hand fast. Does it swing high?

ask.q: What happened when you shook it fast?
good: It just jiggled and stayed small.
The pushes didn't match the swing.

flow.do: Talk about a playground swing.
flow.say: When do you push a friend on a swing, so that they go higher? Why does that work?
flow.kid: When should you push a friend on a swing? Why?

check.q: You push your friend on a swing. When should you push, to make them go higher?
options: Just as they start to swing away from you
While they are still coming towards you
check.why: Pushing as they start to move away adds to their swing. Pushing while they come towards you works against the swing and slows it. Small pushes at the swing's own beat add up. This is resonance.

setup.art: A child's hand holding the top of a thread with a coin bag hanging still below.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the thread. Let the bag hang still.

setup.art: The same hand moving a tiny bit to the side, and the bag swinging wide below it, with a growing curved arrow.
setup.caption: 2. Tiny movements in time make a big swing.

activities.title: Two Pendulums Share a String
activities.context: In this activity you hang two pendulums from one string and watch the swing pass from one to the other and back.

materials.item: two chairs
string, about 1.5 metres
thread, about 1 metre
two small bags with 5 coins each

activities.safety: Put the chairs where nobody will trip over the string.

schedule.what: Hang two equal pendulums from a string between two chairs and watch the swing move between them.

activities.record: Draw the two pendulums at the start, after 30 seconds and after a minute. Show which one is swinging.

flow.do: 1. Put two chairs back to back, about 1 metre apart. 2. Tie the string between the chair backs, a little loose so it sags about 3 cm. 3. Hang two coin pendulums from it, 20 cm apart, each exactly 30 cm long.
flow.say: Two pendulums, the same length, hanging from one string. We start only one.
flow.kid: Hang two pendulums from the string. Make them the same length.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Pendulums Share a String.

flow.do: Hold one bag still. Pull the other towards you and let go, swinging front to back. Let go of the still one. Watch for a minute.
flow.say: Only one is swinging. Watch the other one. What happens?
flow.kid: Start one pendulum. Watch the other one. What happens?

good: The still one started to swing.
The first one stopped, then started again.

flow.parent: Within a minute or so the second one starts swinging and the first nearly stops. Then the swing passes back. If nothing happens, check that the lengths match and the string is a little loose.

flow.do: Make one pendulum 15 cm long and try again.
flow.say: Now they are different lengths. Does the swing still pass across?
flow.kid: Make one short. Start the long one. Does the short one swing?

check.q: Two pendulums hang from one string. One is 30 cm and one is 15 cm. You start the long one. What happens to the short one?
options: It swings the other way round
check.why: Each small tug on the string comes at the long pendulum's beat. That is not the short one's own beat, so the tugs don't add up. Equal lengths have the same beat, so the swing passes fully across. This is resonance again.

setup.caption: 1. Two equal pendulums hang from one loose string.

setup.art: The same setup with the left pendulum still and the right one swinging, and an arrow showing the swing passing across.
setup.caption: 2. Start one. Watch the swing pass to the other.

activities.title: Your Legs Are Pendulums
activities.context: In this activity you find out that your legs swing like pendulums when you walk.

materials.item: a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a grown-up to walk with

activities.safety: Walk in a clear corridor or room, or a building's lobby.

schedule.what: Count your steps and a grown-up's steps in 20 seconds of relaxed walking.

activities.record: Write your steps and the grown-up's steps in 20 seconds. Circle the bigger number.

flow.do: Stand on one foot, holding a wall. Let the other leg hang loose and swing it gently.
flow.say: Let your leg hang and swing. Your hip is the pivot. Your leg is a pendulum.
flow.kid: Hold the wall. Swing one leg gently. Your hip is the pivot.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Legs Are Pendulums.

flow.do: 1. Walk at a relaxed pace for 20 seconds and count your steps. 2. The grown-up does the same. Don't hurry or slow down on purpose.
flow.say: Walk the way you always do. Count your steps for 20 seconds.
flow.kid: Walk normally for 20 seconds. Count every step.

good: I did, because my legs are shorter.
Shorter legs swing quicker, like a short pendulum.

flow.do: Talk about the result.
flow.say: Your legs are shorter pendulums than mine. What does a shorter pendulum do?
flow.kid: Your legs are short pendulums. What do short pendulums do?

check.q: A small child and a tall grown-up walk side by side at a relaxed pace. Who takes quicker steps?
options: They take steps at the same speed
check.why: A leg swings forward like a pendulum. A shorter leg swings quicker, so the child takes quicker steps.

setup.art: A child holding a wall with one hand, swinging one loose leg back and forth.
setup.caption: 1. Swing one leg. Your hip is the pivot.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up walking side by side down a corridor, the child taking two small steps for each of the grown-up's long ones.
setup.caption: 2. Count your steps in 20 seconds. Who takes more?

activities.title: Pendulum Pictures in Salt
activities.context: In this art activity a swinging paper cone full of salt draws patterns on dark paper.

materials.item: a sheet of newspaper or paper, to roll into a cone
about a cup of fine salt or rava
dark paper or a dark cloth, on the floor
string, about 1.5 metres
two chairs and a broom

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the hole. Sweep up the salt afterwards so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Hang a salt cone from a broom across two chairs and let it draw patterns as it swings.

activities.record: Take a photo or draw the pattern. Write how you started the swing.

flow.do: 1. Roll the paper into a cone and tape it. 2. Snip the tip to make a hole about 3 mm wide. 3. Tape three threads round the top rim and tie them together above. 4. Lay the broom across two chair backs. 5. Hang the cone from it on the string, about 5 cm above the dark paper.
flow.say: We are making a pendulum that draws. The salt will fall out of the tip as it swings.
flow.kid: Make a paper cone. Hang it from the broom. Keep a finger on the hole.
flow.parent: If the salt doesn't flow, make the hole a little bigger. If it pours too fast, use fine salt instead of rava.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pendulum Pictures, where a swinging cone of salt draws patterns.

flow.do: 1. Fill the cone with salt, keeping a finger over the hole. 2. Pull it to one side and give it a small sideways push as you let go, so it swings in an oval. 3. Watch the pattern grow.
flow.say: Push it a little sideways as you let go, so it swings round in an oval. Watch what it draws.
flow.kid: Fill the cone. Let go with a little sideways push. Watch it draw!

ask.q: Why do the loops get smaller and smaller?
good: Air resistance and the pivot slow it down.
It loses a bit of swing each time.

flow.do: Pour the salt back in a bowl. Try a straight swing, then an oval, then a big circle.
flow.say: Which start makes which pattern? Can you guess before you let go?
flow.kid: Try a straight swing, then an oval. Guess the pattern first.
flow.parent: A straight swing draws a line that gets shorter. An oval swing draws loops that shrink towards the middle.

setup.art: A paper cone hanging on three threads from a broom laid across two chair backs, above a dark sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a salt cone from a broom across two chairs.

setup.art: Salt trickling from the swinging cone and drawing a pattern of shrinking ovals on the dark paper.
setup.caption: 2. Let it swing in an oval and watch the pattern.

projects.title: A Pendulum Wave
projects.context: In this 2-day project you hang five pendulums of carefully chosen lengths from a broom. Let go of them together, and they make a moving snake pattern, then line up again.

materials.item: a broom or a long stick
two chairs of the same height
strong thread, about 4 metres in all
5 small plastic bags, each with 3 coins of the same kind
sticky tape
a measuring tape
a piece of stiff cardboard as long as the broom
a phone stopwatch

projects.safety: Put the chairs where nobody will walk into the threads.

schedule.what: Hang five pendulums of lengths 39, 33, 28 and a half, 25 and 22 cm from a broom across two chairs.
Check each length by timing, let go of all five together and watch the wave.

projects.record: Draw the pattern at the start, after a few seconds and after 15 seconds. Write how many swings each pendulum made in 15 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Lay the broom across two chair backs. 2. Tie each coin bag with two threads to two points on the broom, 10 cm apart, so it hangs in a V. 3. Hang them 12 cm apart along the broom. 4. Measure straight down from the broom to the middle of the coins. 5. Make the lengths 39, 33, 28 and a half, 25 and 22 cm.
flow.say: Each pendulum is a little shorter than the last. The two threads keep each one swinging only front to back.
flow.kid: Hang five pendulums in a row. Each one is a bit shorter. Measure carefully.
flow.parent: The lengths must be right to about half a centimetre, so measure twice. The V of two threads stops the bags twisting and swinging sideways.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Pendulum Wave project. You hang five pendulums of carefully chosen lengths.

flow.do: 1. Time 10 swings of each pendulum. The longest should take about 12 and a half seconds, the shortest about 9 and a half. 2. Fix any that are off by moving the thread. 3. Use the cardboard to pull all five bags back together. 4. Pull the cardboard away quickly, and watch.
flow.say: Each one swings at its own beat. Watch what pattern they make together. What happens after 15 seconds?
flow.kid: Pull them all back with the card. Let go. Watch the pattern!
flow.wait: Day 2: check the lengths and let go of the wave.
flow.parent: In 15 seconds the longest makes 12 full swings and the shortest makes 16. In between, they spread out into a snake and then lines that cross. At 15 seconds they all line up again. If the pattern is messy, check the lengths.

check.q: In the pendulum wave, which pendulum makes the most swings in 15 seconds?
options: They all make the same number
check.why: The shortest pendulum swings quickest, so it fits the most swings into 15 seconds. That is why they drift apart, then line up again.

challenges.title: The Longest Swinger
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a pendulum that keeps swinging for as long as possible.
challenges.problem: Build a pendulum that keeps swinging as long as possible after one start, without anyone touching it again.
constraints: The pendulum must hang from the ruler on the table, or from a broom across two chairs.
Let go from 20 cm out to the side.
Time it until it no longer swings out 5 cm.
materials: coins, a steel nut, a lemon or a small stone
general: Use a small, heavy bob, such as a bag of many coins, so the air pushes on it very little compared with its weight.
Use a thin thread, and a smooth pivot that doesn't rub.
creative: Hang it from a sharp edge, like the blade of a butter knife taped across two boxes, so the pivot barely rubs.
Make it long. A long pendulum swings slowly, so it moves through the air more gently.
Put it in a cupboard or a quiet room, so no fan or breeze disturbs it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own longest swinger. Draw it, build it and time it. Then change one thing and see if it beats your record.

challenges.problem: Kavya practises Carnatic songs and needs a steady beat. Build a pendulum that can give 60 full swings a minute, and then a quicker beat, without retying any knots.
constraints: No retying knots once it is built.

materials: a ruler and books, or a broom across two chairs
general: Wind the thread round a pencil at the pivot. Turn the pencil to wind it up shorter or let it out longer.
Mark the thread with a pen at the right lengths for each beat.
creative: Thread a bead on the string and pinch the thread against the bead to make the swinging part shorter.
Make a paper scale next to the thread that shows where to set it for slow, medium and quick beats.

flow.parent: About 25 cm gives 60 full swings a minute. About 12 cm gives a quicker beat of about 85 a minute.

quiz.p: On a playground swing, which part is the pivot?
opts: The bar or hooks at the top
quiz.why: The pivot is the fixed point the swing hangs from, at the top. The child on the seat is the bob. Picking the seat means mixing up the bob and the pivot.

quiz.p: Divya lets go of a swing. It goes to the far side and comes back to her hands. How much swinging has it done?
quiz.why: One full swing is there and back again. Counting each side as a swing gives twice the right number.

quiz.p: Where does a pendulum move fastest?
opts: At the bottom, in the middle of its swing
It moves at the same speed all the way
quiz.why: The bob speeds up as it falls towards the middle, and slows down as it climbs. At each end it stops for a moment. If you picked the ends, watch a swing again: it pauses there.

quiz.p: Why does a pendulum not stop at the bottom, where it hangs at rest?
opts: It is moving fast there, so it carries on up the other side
It wants to reach the other side
quiz.why: A moving thing keeps moving unless something slows it. At the bottom the bob is moving fastest, so it carries on up the far side until gravity slows it.

quiz.p: Farhan wants to test if the weight of the bob changes the swing time. What should he change?
opts: The weight and the length together
Only the weight, keeping the same length and start
quiz.why: In a fair test you change one thing only. If Farhan changed the length too, he would not know which change made the difference.

quiz.p: Why do we time 10 full swings instead of just one?
opts: One swing is too quick to time well, so a small stopwatch mistake matters less over 10
Because the first nine don't count
quiz.why: One swing takes about a second, and pressing a stopwatch can be off by a few tenths of a second. Over 10 swings, the same mistake is a much smaller part of the time.

quiz.p: Lakshmi swings 5 coins on a 50 cm thread. Then she takes out 4 coins, leaving 1, and keeps the length the same. What happens to the time for 10 swings?
quiz.why: The weight changes the time very little. Gravity pulls the heavier bob harder, but it also needs more force to move. Thinking it changes a lot is the most common first guess.

quiz.p: Meena makes her pendulum's thread a quarter as long. Before, 10 swings took 14 seconds. About how long do they take now?
quiz.why: Making a pendulum 4 times shorter makes it swing twice as fast. Half of 14 seconds is 7 seconds. Many people expect a quarter of the time, but the length and the time do not change in step.

quiz.p: Arjun pushes his little sister on a swing, first gently and then much harder. What happens to the time for each swing?
opts: It stays nearly the same, but the swing goes higher
quiz.why: A harder push sends the swing further and faster, and the two balance out. Each swing takes nearly the same time. Only very wide swings take a little longer.

quiz.p: Why does a pendulum with a big card taped on it stop swinging sooner?
opts: The air pushes against the big flat card
The card makes the string shorter
The card makes it swing quicker
quiz.why: The card pushes a lot of air out of the way, and the air pushes back. That is air resistance. A card weighs very little.

quiz.p: You push a friend on a swing. When should you push to make them go higher?
opts: While they are still coming towards you
Just as they start to move away from you
Only when they are at the bottom, moving fast
quiz.why: Pushes that come at the swing's own beat, as it moves away, add up and make it grow. This is resonance. A push while they come towards you slows them down.

quiz.p: A pendulum wall clock is running slow. What should you do to the pendulum?
quiz.why: A shorter pendulum swings quicker, so the clock ticks faster and catches up. Most clocks have a small nut under the bob that moves it up or down.

quiz.p: Hoolock gibbons live high in the trees of Assam. How do they travel fast from tree to tree without coming down?
opts: They swing from one long arm to the other, like a pendulum
quiz.why: Gibbons hang from one long arm and swing forward like a pendulum to the next branch. Gravity does much of the work, so it saves energy.

items.p: Label the three parts of this pendulum: pivot, string and bob.
items.why: The pivot is the fixed point at the top. The bob is the weight at the bottom. A strong answer also says that the length is measured from the pivot to the middle of the bob.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: a weight hanging from a fixed point, free to swing
the fixed point a pendulum hangs from
the weight at the bottom of a pendulum
the push of air against a moving thing
small pushes at the swing's own beat adding up

items.p: Sort these things. Is each one a pendulum, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: A pendulum hangs from one fixed point and swings freely. A ceiling fan turns in circles, and a ball rolling down a slope does not swing back and forth.
items: a bunch of keys hanging on a ring
a ball rolling down a slope

items.p: Kavya says, 'A heavier bob makes a pendulum swing faster.' Is she right?
items.why: False. In the Swing Test, 1 coin and 5 coins took about the same time for 10 swings. A strong answer gives the numbers from the test.

items.p: A pendulum stops for a moment at each end of its swing.
items.why: True. At each end it has climbed as high as it can go, so it stops for a moment before gravity pulls it back.

items.p: A pendulum moves fastest at the ______ of its swing.
items.why: It speeds up on the way down and slows down on the way up, so it is fastest at the bottom.

items.p: To make a pendulum swing quicker, make its string ______.
items.why: A shorter pendulum swings quicker. Adding weight hardly changes it.

items.p: Sneha's pendulum takes 14 seconds for 10 swings. She starts it from twice as far out to the side. About how long will 10 swings take now?
items.why: A wider start makes the bob travel further, but also faster, so the time stays about the same. It may be a few tenths of a second longer.

items.p: Put the steps of the Swing Test for weight in order.
a: Build a 50 cm pendulum with 5 coins
Take out 4 coins and keep the length 50 cm
Time 10 swings again, twice, and compare
items.why: First build it, then time it, then change only the weight, then time and compare.
items: Time 10 swings again, twice, and compare
Build a 50 cm pendulum with 5 coins
Take out 4 coins and keep the length 50 cm

items.p: Explain why a pendulum keeps swinging past the middle instead of stopping there.
items.a: At the middle the bob is moving fastest. A moving thing keeps going unless something slows it, so it carries on up the other side until gravity slows it to a stop.
items.why: A strong answer says the bob is moving fast at the middle, and that gravity slows it on the way up.

items.p: Your friend counts each side of a swing as one swing. You count there and back as one. Whose count of 10 swings will take longer? Why?
items.a: Mine, because each of my swings is two of my friend's. My 10 swings take twice as long as theirs.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the two ways of counting differ by two times, and says why everyone must count the same way to compare.

items.p: Draw a pendulum at the start, the middle and the far end of one swing. Draw a long arrow where it moves fastest and no arrow where it stops.
items.a: A long arrow at the bottom and no arrows at the two ends.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bob fastest at the bottom and still for a moment at each end.
items.art: Three blank pivot points with space below each.

items.p: Two cousins in Hyderabad are on the swings in their building's play area.
items.a: A strong answer uses the Swing Test, where weight changed the time very little, so Ayesha is right that the beat stays the same. It also gives Rohan his due: he is right that his swing goes higher with a big push.
items.why: This question checks that the child can tell 'goes higher' apart from 'swings quicker', and uses evidence.

views.says: If my big sister sits on the swing, it will go back and forth faster, because she is heavier.
Heavy or light, each swing takes about the same time. Only a push makes it go higher, not quicker.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you found in the Swing Test. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.

items.p: Why does a swing slow down and stop if nobody pushes it?
items.why: Each swing, the air pushes back and the hooks rub on the bar. Gravity does not tire. Picking 'gravity gets tired' means thinking of gravity as something that runs out.
opts: Air resistance and friction at the hooks slow it a little on each swing

items.p: Three of these change how long a pendulum takes to swing very little. Which one changes it a lot?
items.why: The length sets the beat. The weight, a small start and a slightly wider start change it very little.

items.p: Rani has a pendulum 1 metre long. Each full swing takes about 2 seconds. How long should she make it so each swing takes about 1 second?
items.why: To halve the time, make the pendulum a quarter as long. A quarter of 1 metre is 25 cm. Many people guess half the length, 50 cm, but that makes it only a little quicker.

items.p: A very wide swing, let go from almost level with the pivot, takes a little longer than a small swing.
items.why: True. Christiaan Huygens worked this out in 1673. For a swing let go from level with the pivot, each swing takes about one sixth longer. For small swings the difference is tiny.

items.p: In the One-Second Pendulum, many children first guess about 30 cm, halfway between 12 and a half cm and 50 cm. Why is the right length shorter than halfway?
items.a: The time does not change in step with the length. A quarter of the length gives half the time, so to get from 7 seconds to 10 seconds you need less extra length than you might think. The answer is about 25 cm.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers from the experiments and says that length and time do not change by the same amount.

items.p: Sort these changes. Will each one make a swing die down sooner, or make little difference?
items.a: see items
items.why: Things that push more air, or rub more at the pivot, make it die down sooner. A heavy, small bob is slowed least.
items: taping a postcard to the bob
a big, light balloon as the bob

items.p: Two pendulums hang from one loose string. Both are 30 cm long. You start one. What will the other one do?
items.why: Each small tug on the string comes at the first pendulum's beat, which is also the second one's own beat. So the tugs add up, and the swing passes across. This is resonance.
opts: Swing the opposite way at once
Slowly start swinging, while the first one slows down

items.p: Why does pushing a swing at the wrong moment, while it is still coming towards you, make it go lower?
items.a: The push is against the way the swing is moving, so it slows the swing down instead of adding to it.
items.why: A strong answer says the push and the movement are in opposite directions.

items.p: Draw a parent pushing a child on a swing at the best moment. Draw an arrow for the push and an arrow for the way the swing is moving.
items.a: The parent pushes at the back of the swing, as it starts to move away. Both arrows point the same way.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the push and the movement in the same direction.
items.art: A blank swing frame with a swing seat.

items.p: Two scientists from long ago disagree about pendulums.
items.a: A strong answer says Galileo was right for small swings: weight hardly matters and small swings take nearly the same time. It says Huygens was right that very wide swings take a little longer, and that clockmakers keep swings small. Both used careful thinking and tests.
items.why: This checks that the child sees that an idea can be nearly right, and how a better test or better maths improves it.

views.says: A pendulum takes the same time for every swing, small or wide.
Small swings take nearly the same time. But very wide swings take a little longer.

items.ask: Who was right? Use what you found when you tried a small and a wide start. Then say what the other scientist got right.

items.p: When small pushes come at a swing's own beat and add up, it is called ______.
items.why: Resonance is why a few small pushes can make a swing go very high.

items.p: Match each pendulum to about how long it takes for one full swing.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A longer pendulum takes longer for each swing. A jhumka is tiny, so it swings quickest.
pairs: A jhumka on a 3 cm hook

items.p: Put these pendulums in order, from the one that swings quickest to the one that swings slowest.
items.why: Only the length decides the order. The coins do not change it.

items.p: On this drawing of a swing, label where the swing moves fastest, and the two places where it stops for a moment.
items.why: A strong answer puts 'fastest' at the lowest point and 'stops' at each end.
items.art: A curved path of a swing with three blank label lines at the bottom and both ends.

items.p: On the Moon, where gravity is weaker, the same pendulum would swing more slowly.
items.why: True. Gravity pulls the bob back towards the middle. Weaker gravity pulls it back more gently, so each swing takes longer, about two and a half times as long.

items.p: Your legs swing like pendulums when you walk. Who takes quicker steps when walking relaxed, a small child or a tall grown-up?
items.why: A child's legs are shorter pendulums, so they swing forward quicker. That is why a child takes more steps to keep up.

items.p: Megha's wall clock is 2 minutes fast every day. What should she do to the pendulum, and why?
items.a: Make it a tiny bit longer by moving the bob down with the nut. A longer pendulum swings slower, so the clock ticks slower and stops gaining time.
items.why: A strong answer says 'longer' and gives the reason: longer swings slower.

items.p: Gravity pulls a heavy bob harder than a light one. So why does the heavy bob not swing faster?
items.a: A heavy bob also needs more force to get moving, just as a full trolley is harder to push than an empty one. The extra pull and the extra mass cancel out, so both swing at the same beat.
items.why: A strong answer names both sides: the bigger pull and the bigger mass, and says they cancel.

items.p: A wide swing travels much further than a small one. How can it take almost the same time?
items.a: Let go from further out, the bob falls from higher, so it moves faster. It travels further, but faster, so the time stays almost the same.
items.why: A strong answer links the longer path to the faster speed.

items.p: Three people talk about why a swing in a park stopped.
items.a: A strong answer agrees most with Selvi, because the card test showed air slowing a pendulum, and a squeaky swing loses movement at its hooks. It gives Nisha her due: gravity does keep pulling, but it pulls the swing back to the middle, it does not stop it. And it gives Ravi his due: the swing did move less and less, but the movement went somewhere, into warmth.
items.why: This checks that the child can use the card test as evidence and judge three ideas fairly.

views.says: Gravity pulled it down, so it stopped.
The air pushed against it and the hooks rubbed, so it slowed a little every swing.
Its movement just ran out, like a phone battery.

items.ask: Which idea explains it best? Use the card test as evidence. Then say what each of the others got partly right.

items.p: In the pendulum wave, the longest pendulum makes 12 swings in 15 seconds and the shortest makes 16. Why do they all line up again at 15 seconds?
items.why: Each pendulum makes a whole number of swings in 15 seconds, so at that moment every one is back where it started. In between they are out of step.
opts: Because each one has made a whole number of swings and is back at the start
Because the air pushes them back together

items.p: Santorio Santorio, an Italian doctor in the early 1600s, measured his patients' pulse with a pendulum. He changed its length until each swing matched a heartbeat. How could the length tell him how fast the heart was beating?
items.a: A shorter pendulum swings quicker. So a quick pulse matched a short pendulum, and a slow pulse matched a long one. By reading the length, he could compare pulses from day to day.
items.why: A strong answer links short to quick and long to slow, and says the length becomes a measure.

items.p: Draw a graph with length on the bottom and the time for 10 swings up the side. Plot 12 and a half cm at 7 seconds, 25 cm at 10 seconds and 50 cm at 14 seconds. Join the points. Is it a straight line?
items.a: The points rise, but the line bends and gets flatter. It is not a straight line.
items.why: A strong answer sees that doubling the length does not double the time.
items.art: A blank graph grid with axes labelled length in cm and seconds for 10 swings.

items.p: A clock pendulum swings only a few centimetres each way. Why do clockmakers keep the swing so small?
items.why: Very wide swings take a little longer, and the time changes if the width changes. Small swings all take nearly the same time, so the clock stays steady.
opts: Small swings all take nearly the same time, so the clock stays accurate
Small swings use a lighter bob

items.p: Equal-length pendulums hanging from one string pass their swing back and forth, but a short and a long one hardly do.
items.why: True. The tugs through the string come at one pendulum's beat. Only a pendulum with the same beat takes them up and grows. This is resonance.

items.p: Many people think a bigger push makes a swing go back and forth quicker. Plan a test to find out if they are right. Say what you change, what you keep the same and what you measure.
items.a: Change only how far out you let it go. Keep the same length and the same bob. Time 10 swings from each start, twice each.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, measures 10 swings and repeats.

items.p: Sort these into what sets a pendulum's beat a lot, and what changes it very little.
items.a: see items
items.why: The length and gravity set the beat. The weight, the material and the size of a small start change it very little.
items: a brass bob instead of a steel one
a small start or a slightly wider one

items.p: A pendulum about ______ long takes one second to swing one way, so tall floor clocks use one this long.
items.why: A pendulum about 1 metre long takes 1 second each way, and 2 seconds for a full swing there and back.

items.p: A metronome is a pendulum turned upside down, with a sliding weight on its arm. A music teacher slides the weight up. What happens?
items.why: Sliding the weight up makes the metronome tick more slowly, a bit like making a pendulum longer.

items.p: On a drawing of a pendulum clock, label the pendulum, the bob, the nut that moves the bob, and the wheel that ticks.
items.why: A strong answer also says which way to turn the nut, up for faster and down for slower.
items.art: A simple drawing of the inside of a wall clock with four blank labels.

items.p: Three of these use a swing or a back-and-forth beat to keep time. Which one does not?
items.why: A sundial uses the Sun's shadow. A pendulum clock, a metronome and a quartz watch, whose crystal vibrates 32,768 times a second, all count a steady back-and-forth beat.

items.p: Hoolock gibbons swing through the treetops like pendulums. Why does this way of travelling help them find fruit high in the forest?
items.a: They can cross from tree to tree fast without coming down to the ground. Swinging lets gravity do much of the work, so it saves energy for a long day of looking for fruit.
items.why: A strong answer says what problem the gibbon has, staying high and travelling far, and how swinging helps.

applications: Pendulum clocks were the most accurate clocks in the world for nearly 300 years, from 1656 until the 1930s.
Musicians practise with metronomes, which keep a steady beat with a swinging arm.
Playground swings, cradles and the Onam oonjal are pendulums. Children pump them higher by moving in time with the swing.
Engineers design tall buildings and bridges so that wind and footsteps do not push them at their own beat and make them sway.
Some tall buildings hang a huge heavy weight near the top. It swings against the sway and calms the building in strong winds.
Scientists once measured the strength of gravity in different places by timing very exact pendulums.
Doctors in the early 1600s used pendulums to compare how fast a patient's pulse was beating.
Every clock counts a steady back-and-forth beat: a pendulum, the quartz crystal in a watch, or atoms in an atomic clock.

open_questions.q: What is time, really? Does it flow on its own, or is it only the order in which things happen?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists and philosophers still argue about this. Clocks measure time very exactly, but nobody agrees on what it is.

open_questions.q: Why do some swinging things, like metronomes on a shared board, fall into step with each other?
open_questions.why_open: The basic idea is understood, but how large groups of swinging things fall into step is still being studied. In 1665, Christiaan Huygens saw two of his pendulum clocks on one beam fall into step, and scientists still study this today.

open_questions.q: How do our bodies keep their own beats, like the heartbeat and the daily sleep rhythm, so steady?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the cells and signals involved, but not everything about how they stay so steady over a whole lifetime.

open_questions.q: Two pendulums joined together, one hanging from the other, swing in wild patterns that never repeat. Can we ever predict them exactly?
open_questions.why_open: This double pendulum follows simple rules, but the tiniest change at the start makes a big difference later. So in practice, nobody can predict it for long.
