maths.problem: In the Swing Test, 10 full swings of the 50 cm pendulum took 14 seconds. About how long did one full swing take?
maths.answer: About 1 and a half seconds. More exactly, 1.4 seconds.
maths.explain: One swing is one tenth of 10 swings. 14 seconds shared into 10 equal parts is 1.4 seconds each. That is a little less than one and a half seconds.
maths.context: This is about the Swing Test, where you timed 10 full swings of a coin pendulum on a 50 cm thread.
maths.why_maths: Timing 10 swings and sharing by 10 gives a much more exact time for one swing than timing one swing alone.

maths.problem: A pendulum takes 1 second for each full swing. How many full swings does it make in 3 minutes?
maths.explain: There are 60 seconds in a minute, so 60 swings in a minute. In 3 minutes there are 60 + 60 + 60 = 180 seconds, so 180 swings.
maths.context: This is about the One-Second Pendulum, where you set the thread so each full swing takes 1 second.
maths.why_maths: A clock is a counter of swings. Changing minutes into seconds tells you how many swings it must count.

maths.problem: Here is a pattern. A pendulum 25 cm long takes 1 second for each swing. One 4 times as long, 1 metre, takes 2 seconds. One 4 times longer again, 4 metres, takes 4 seconds. How long would a 16 metre pendulum take?
maths.explain: Each time the length is multiplied by 4, the time is multiplied by 2. 4 metres times 4 is 16 metres. 4 seconds times 2 is 8 seconds.
maths.context: This is about the swing time and the length of a pendulum, from the explanation card on length.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict the swing time of a pendulum far too long to build at home.

maths.problem: Ishani timed 10 swings with 5 coins: 14.1 and 14.4 seconds. With 1 coin: 14.3 and 14.0 seconds. Her brother says the 1 coin was quicker, because 14.0 is less than 14.1. Is he right to say so?
maths.answer: No. The two tries with 1 coin added up to 28.3 seconds, and with 5 coins 28.5 seconds. That is only 0.2 seconds apart, which is less than the difference between two tries of the same pendulum. So the weight made no difference she could measure.
maths.explain: 14.1 + 14.4 = 28.5. 14.3 + 14.0 = 28.3. The two 5-coin tries differ by 0.3 seconds on their own. A difference smaller than that is just the stopwatch, not the coins.
maths.context: This is about the Swing Test for weight, where you time 10 swings with 5 coins and then with 1 coin.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a difference with how much your own tries vary tells you whether a change is real or only a timing slip.

maths.problem: In the Pendulum Wave, the longest pendulum makes 12 swings in 15 seconds and the shortest makes 16. How many more swings does the shortest make in 30 seconds?
maths.explain: In 30 seconds, twice as long, the longest makes 24 swings and the shortest makes 32. 32 - 24 = 8.
maths.context: This is about the Pendulum Wave project, where five pendulums of different lengths swing side by side.
maths.why_maths: Doubling the counts shows how far apart the pendulums drift, and why they line up again at each 15 seconds.

roots.context: We have learned that a pendulum's beat is set by its length, and how clocks count that beat. Now we ask what swings tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Ten swings took about the same time with one coin or five, from a small start or a wide one. Only a shorter string made the swings quicker. The length and the Earth's pull set the beat, and your push only sets how wide it swings. So every pendulum of one length keeps the same time here, and that is how clocks were made.
deep_truth.habit: We expect a bigger push or a heavier weight to make things go faster, as if speed always comes from effort. A pendulum keeps its own beat whatever we do to it. The steady time of a clock was not made by people. Clockmakers found a beat that the Earth's pull and a length of string already keep, and counted it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Swing Test, 1 coin and 5 coins both took about 14 seconds for 10 swings, and so did a wide start. A thread a quarter as long took about 7 seconds.

three.who_am_i: Your legs swing like pendulums when you walk. Your heart and your breathing keep their own beats too.
three.what_is_life: Hoolock gibbons in the forests of Assam swing through the trees like pendulums, letting gravity carry them to the next branch.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth's pull sets the beat of every pendulum on it. On the Moon, the same pendulum would swing about two and a half times more slowly.

roots.thread: A pendulum at rest hangs straight down, perfectly balanced. Pull it to one side and let go, and it swings across to the other side and back. Every swing to the left is matched by a swing to the right, around that still middle. Out of one still balance comes a rhythm that repeats again and again. People counted that rhythm and turned it into hours, days and calendars that a whole world shares.

teachings.teaching: Returning is the movement of the Tao.
teachings.link: A pendulum always turns back towards its middle. Its whole movement is made of going out and returning.

teachings.teaching: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain, come and go. They do not last. Bear them patiently.
teachings.link: A swing goes up on one side and up on the other, but its resting point stays where it is. The swing changes all the time around a middle that does not move.

science.text: Every clock counts a steady back-and-forth beat. A quartz watch counts a crystal that vibrates 32,768 times a second. The second itself is defined as 9,192,631,770 waves of a kind of light given out by caesium atoms.
What time itself is, and whether it flows on its own, is still argued about by physicists and philosophers.

other_view.view: Newton thought time flows evenly by itself, even if nothing moves at all, and clocks only measure it. Leibniz disagreed. He said there is no time apart from things happening, and time is only the order in which they happen. Many scientists today say a pendulum is just gravity and a string, and the rhythm is in our counting, not in nature.

practice.title: Breathe with the pendulum
practice.say: Let's hang our 50 cm pendulum and start it with a small swing. Sit still and watch it. Breathe in slowly while it makes three swings. Breathe out slowly while it makes three more. playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed, and the times worked out from the pendulum rule (a 25 cm pendulum takes about 1 second for a full swing). The coin pendulum hangs from a ruler held down by books on a dining table, so it works in any flat. The bag of coins keeps the weight in one small place, so 1 coin and 5 coins hang at the same length when measured to the middle of the coins. At 50 cm, 10 swings take about 14 seconds and at 12 and a half cm about 7, a difference no child can miss. A start of 25 cm out from a 50 cm pendulum is about 30 degrees, which adds only about 2 percent, a few tenths of a second over 10 swings, so the child sees 'about the same'. Counting is the most common mistake, so step 2 teaches 'zero' on letting go and one for each return. The card test makes the swing die down in well under a minute, against a minute or more without it. The two pendulums on a string need equal lengths and a slightly loose string. The salt cone needs a hole about 3 mm wide. Both games work for one child. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: Does a wide swing take longer than a small one? This card tells how people found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, and Christiaan Huygens, a Dutch scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1602 (Galileo's letter) to 1673 (Huygens's book on pendulum clocks)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Galileo thought every swing of a pendulum takes exactly the same time, however wide. Huygens showed that very wide swings take a little longer.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1602, Galileo Galilei was teaching in Padua, in Italy. He wrote to a friend, Guidobaldo del Monte, about his tests with pendulums. He had hung two balls on threads of the same length, one of heavy lead and one of light cork. He pulled them aside together and let them go. They kept swinging back and forth together, the heavy one and the light one in step. Galileo also said that a swing takes the same time whether it is wide or small. He thought this was exactly true for every swing, even very wide ones. In 1656, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens used this steady beat to build the first pendulum clock. It kept time far better than any clock before it. But Huygens worked carefully through the mathematics of the swing. In his book of 1673, he showed that Galileo was not quite right. A very wide swing takes a little longer than a small one. For small swings the difference is tiny. That is why the pendulum in a clock swings only a little way each side.
